claims.text: Wear resistance of HEA coatings on transition-metal matrices has a non-monotonic dependence on ambient temperature.
The initial increase in wear resistance with temperature is caused by thermally activated solid-solution strengthening.
The initial increase in wear resistance with temperature is also caused by oxide-film formation.
Above a critical temperature, wear resistance degrades sharply because thermal softening and diffusion-driven phase instability become dominant.
The coating is initially in a metastable solid-solution or multiphase state under ambient conditions.
Temperature variation causes evolution involving thermally activated dislocation glide and dynamic recrystallization.
Temperature variation promotes formation of a protective tribo-oxide layer.
High configurational entropy and lattice distortion impede dislocation motion at lower to moderate temperatures.
Moderate heating promotes formation of a continuous, adherent oxide layer.
A continuous, adherent oxide layer reduces friction.
Above a critical temperature, thermal softening reduces the coating's yield strength.
Accelerated diffusion at high temperature causes phase decomposition or grain growth.
High-temperature microstructural changes cause the protective oxide layer to become porous or spall.
Breakdown of the protective oxide layer leads to severe adhesive and abrasive wear.
Wear resistance reaches a maximum, corresponding to a minimum wear rate, at approximately 300–500 °C.
Wear rates increase at very low temperatures because of brittle fracture.
Wear rates increase at high temperatures because of thermal softening and oxide instability.
The degradation boundary is operationally defined as the temperature at which wear rate exceeds its room-temperature value by a factor of two or coefficient of friction rises by more than 50%.

contradictions.description: The conditions allow either inert gas or air while claiming this isolates thermal effects from environmental oxidation. These atmospheres have substantially different access to oxidation, yet protective tribo-oxide formation and breakdown are central mediators in the proposed mechanism.
The intervention describes a range extending from cryogenic temperatures but gives 25–800 °C as its example range; 25 °C is not cryogenic.
